title: America grounded every plane. What if the whole world did?

scenes.narration: Yesterday, America stopped every plane from taking off. For four hours and 21 minutes, the busiest skies on Earth went quiet. It has happened only three times in history.
At 3:54 in the afternoon, the links between air traffic control centres started failing. Old routers, overloaded with data, began giving inconsistent readings.
More than 3,500 planes were already in the sky, and they landed safely. But 11,000 more flights, carrying one and a half million people, were due to take off.
By the end, nearly 8,000 flights were cancelled and more than 10,000 delayed. The last time this happened was in 2023. Before that, 9/11.
On 9/11, controllers landed more than 4,500 planes in three hours. 38 jets came down in Gander, a Canadian town of under 10,000 people.
So what if it happened everywhere at once? Somewhere between 10,000 and 24,000 planes are in the air at any moment. Let's land them all.

elements.text: What if the whole world stopped?

scenes.narration: Minute one. Every pilot gets the same order: land at the nearest airport. A plane halfway across the ocean has nowhere close to go.
Hour two. Small airports fill up first. Jets park on taxiways, then on runways, wingtip to wingtip, like Gander, but in thousands of towns.
Hour six. Millions of passengers are stuck in places they never meant to visit. Hotels fill in minutes. Trains and buses are swamped.
Day two. Air cargo stops too. Medicines, spare parts and fresh food that fly overnight don't arrive. And restarting is the hard part: every plane and crew is in the wrong city.

elements.text: Planes and crews in the wrong cities

scenes.narration: Back to reality. Yesterday's four hours are still cancelling flights this weekend. And the US Transport Secretary warned: you will have more of these, unless the old system is replaced.
